questions.stem: About electrical and chemical synapses:
options: In an electrical synapse, ions pass directly from one cell to the other through the channels of communicating (gap) junctions
In an electrical synapse, transmission is bidirectional
In a chemical synapse, information passes only from the presynaptic to the postsynaptic element
In an electrical synapse, a neurotransmitter is released into the synaptic cleft
questions.explanation: Chemical synapses are one-way; electrical synapses transmit potential variations directly (ions through gap-junction channels) and are bidirectional. Only chemical synapses use a neurotransmitter.

questions.stem: Among the properties of chemical synapses:
options: The postsynaptic neuron only relays the information without modifying it
They obey the all-or-nothing law
There is a synaptic delay, the time needed to release the neurotransmitter and for it to act on the postsynaptic receptor
Transmission is unidirectional
questions.explanation: Chemical synapses are unidirectional, show fatigue and synaptic delay, have an integrative role (the information can be modified) and do not obey the all-or-nothing law.

questions.stem: During repeated high-frequency stimulation of a presynaptic neuron, the postsynaptic response progressively decreases. This corresponds to:
options: Synaptic delay
Synaptic fatigue, by exhaustion of the neurotransmitter stock
The all-or-nothing law
The integrative role of the synapse
questions.explanation: Fatigue: repeated stimulations lead to a progressive decrease of the postsynaptic response by exhaustion of the neurotransmitter stock. Synaptic delay is a fixed time lag, not a decrement.

questions.stem: In the functioning of a chemical synapse:
options: The neurotransmitter is rapidly inactivated by degradation, recapture or diffusion
Sodium entry is the direct trigger of vesicle exocytosis
The arrival of the action potential at the presynaptic terminal causes calcium entry
The calcium signal triggers exocytosis by membrane fusion
questions.explanation: Sequence: AP → Ca²⁺ entry → exocytosis by fusion → release into the cleft → binding to a specific receptor → rapid inactivation (degradation, recapture, diffusion). It is Ca²⁺, not Na⁺, that triggers release.

questions.stem: Once acetylcholine has acted on the motor end-plate, its action is terminated by:
options: Recapture of choline into the presynaptic terminal by active transporters
Hydrolysis by acetylcholinesterase into choline and acetic acid
Reuptake of intact acetylcholine by the muscle fiber
Degradation by choline acetyltransferase
questions.explanation: ACh is quickly degraded by acetylcholinesterase into choline and acetic acid; choline is recaptured by the presynaptic terminal via active transporters. Choline acetyltransferase synthesizes ACh, it does not degrade it.

questions.stem: About the elements of the synaptic complex:
options: Axo-axonic synapses are neuro-effector synapses
The presynaptic element can be a glandular cell
In a neuro-effector synapse, the postsynaptic element can be a skeletal or cardiac striated muscle cell
In a neuro-effector synapse, the postsynaptic element can be a smooth muscle or glandular cell
questions.explanation: The presynaptic element is always a nerve cell; the postsynaptic one is a neuron (axo-somatic, axo-dendritic, axo-axonic = neuro-neuronal) or an effector (striated, smooth muscle, gland).

questions.stem: About the classification of synapses:
options: In an inhibitory synapse, activation of the presynaptic element hyperpolarizes the postsynaptic membrane
Cholinergic, dopaminergic and peptidergic synapses are classified according to the chemical mediator released
Glutamatergic synapses release gamma-aminobutyric acid
In an excitatory synapse, activation of the presynaptic element depolarizes the postsynaptic membrane
questions.explanation: By effect: excitatory = depolarization, inhibitory = hyperpolarization. By mediator: cholinergic (ACh), glutamatergic (glutamate), GABAergic (GABA), dopaminergic, peptidergic. GABA is released by GABAergic synapses, not glutamatergic ones.

questions.stem: For a molecule to be considered a neurotransmitter, it must:
options: Be specifically inactivated
Be synthesized by the neuron
Reproduce the effect of the endogenous neurotransmitter when applied directly to the target neuron
Be present in the presynaptic terminal
questions.explanation: All four are criteria listed in the course, together with being released in sufficient quantity to act on the postsynaptic neuron.

questions.stem: Which of the following are monoamines?
options: Dopamine
Glutamate
Acetylcholine
Histamine
questions.explanation: Monoamines: noradrenaline, adrenaline, dopamine, serotonin, histamine. Acetylcholine forms its own group and glutamate is an amino acid.

questions.stem: Belong to the 'other' (non-classic) neurotransmitters:
options: Nitric oxide (NO)
Glycine
ATP and adenosine
Peptides
questions.explanation: Non-classic neurotransmitters are mainly peptides, plus NO and ATP/adenosine. Glycine is a classic amino-acid neurotransmitter.

questions.stem: About the structure of the neuromuscular junction:
options: The postsynaptic receptors are muscarinic acetylcholine receptors
It is the contact between the axon of an α motor neuron and a skeletal striated muscle fiber
The synaptic cleft is 50 to 100 nm wide
Each terminal branch of the motor axon innervates several muscle fibers
questions.explanation: Each axon branch innervates a single muscle fiber; the cleft is 50–100 nm; the muscle membrane carries nicotinic ACh receptors at the crests of the junctional folds.

questions.stem: In a nerve–muscle preparation treated with curare or tetrodotoxin (TTX), stimulation of the motor nerve:
options: Produces a potential that reaches threshold and propagates along the muscle fiber
Reveals a local depolarization of the end-plate, the end-plate potential (EPP)
Produces a potential that peaks in about 2 ms and decays exponentially to zero in about 20 ms
No longer triggers a propagated muscle action potential
questions.explanation: Normally nerve stimulation always triggers a muscle AP; after curarization or TTX block only the EPP remains: a local phenomenon peaking at 2 ms and back to zero in 20 ms.

questions.stem: Ionic mechanism of the end-plate potential (voltage-clamp experiment):
options: The EPP is due to an entry of Cl⁻
The resulting potential is an intermediate value around −15 mV
The EPP is due to a simultaneous increase in Na⁺ and K⁺ conductances
Membrane resistance increases during the EPP
questions.explanation: During the EPP membrane resistance decreases as permeabilities increase. Na⁺ and K⁺ each tend toward their equilibrium potential, giving an intermediate value around −15 mV.

questions.stem: Miniature end-plate potentials (MEPPs):
options: Have an amplitude of about 0.5 mV
Result from the release of small amounts (quanta) of acetylcholine
Are recorded without any nerve stimulation
Occur at regular intervals
questions.explanation: MEPPs are small (0.5 mV) spontaneous potentials occurring randomly, not regularly, attributed to the release of quanta of ACh.

questions.stem: Synthesis of acetylcholine:
options: Uses acetyl-coenzyme A and choline
Takes place in the synaptic cleft
Is catalyzed by choline acetyltransferase (CAT)
Takes place in the cytosol of the presynaptic nerve ending
questions.explanation: ACh is made in the cytosol of the presynaptic ending from acetyl-CoA (from mitochondrial glucose metabolism) and choline, by choline acetyltransferase; it is then stored in vesicles.

questions.stem: The ion whose entry into the motor nerve terminal triggers acetylcholine exocytosis is:
options: Ca²⁺
Na⁺
K⁺
Cl⁻
questions.explanation: The presynaptic AP rapidly opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels; Ca²⁺ entry triggers vesicle fusion and exocytosis.

questions.stem: Molecular mechanism of exocytosis:
options: Synaptotagmin, activated by Ca²⁺, is a protein of the plasma membrane
The SNARE complex allows docking of the vesicles and fusion of the vesicular and plasma membranes
Synaptobrevin is a vesicular protein
Syntaxin and SNAP25 belong to the plasma membrane
questions.explanation: Synaptotagmin and synaptobrevin are vesicular; syntaxin and SNAP25 are plasma-membrane SNAREs. Together they dock the vesicle and fuse the membranes.

questions.stem: The muscle nicotinic acetylcholine receptor:
options: When open, increases the membrane permeability to Na⁺ and K⁺
Is a glycoprotein of 5 subunits forming the walls of a central pore
Contains two α subunits
Opens as soon as a single molecule of acetylcholine binds
questions.explanation: The receptor has 5 subunits (2α, β, γ, δ). Binding of two ACh molecules switches it from closed to open, causing a rapid, transient increase in cation (Na⁺, K⁺) permeability.

questions.stem: A patient receives curare during surgery. Curare:
options: Blocks the release of acetylcholine from the nerve ending
Is a reversible competitive antagonist of acetylcholine at the motor end-plate
Is an acetylcholine agonist like suxamethonium
Is a non-depolarizing blocking agent
questions.explanation: Curare acts post-synaptically as a reversible competitive antagonist (non-depolarizing blocker). Suxamethonium is a depolarizing agonist; release is blocked by other agents (Mg²⁺, botulinum toxin…).

questions.stem: Agents that block the release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction:
options: Hemicholinium
Aminoglycoside antibiotics (streptomycin, neomycin)
Botulinum toxin
Mg²⁺
questions.explanation: Release is blocked by Ca²⁺-entry inhibitors (Mg²⁺, aminoglycosides, Ca²⁺-channel blockers) and neurotoxins (botulinum toxin, β-bungarotoxin). Hemicholinium inhibits ACh synthesis.

questions.stem: Which drug–mechanism pairs are correct?
options: Hemicholinium – inhibition of acetylcholine synthesis
α-bungarotoxin – irreversible competitive antagonist
Vesamicol – depolarizing blocking agent
Suxamethonium – acetylcholine agonist (depolarizing blocker)
questions.explanation: Hemicholinium and vesamicol inhibit ACh synthesis; α-bungarotoxin is an irreversible competitive antagonist; decamethonium and suxamethonium are depolarizing agonists.

questions.stem: A patient has autoantibodies against the presynaptic calcium channels of the neuromuscular junction:
options: It is a presynaptic disorder
This is Lambert–Eaton syndrome
Botulism is also a presynaptic disorder, the toxin blocking acetylcholine release
This is myasthenia gravis
questions.explanation: Lambert–Eaton (anti-Ca²⁺ channel antibodies) and botulism are presynaptic disorders. Myasthenia gravis is postsynaptic, with antibodies against ACh receptors.

questions.stem: The excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP):
options: Has an amplitude that depends on the amount of neurotransmitter released
Obeys the all-or-nothing law
Has no refractory period
Is a local depolarization of the postsynaptic membrane
questions.explanation: The EPSP is local, summable, gradable (amplitude depends on the NT amount) and decremental; it does not obey the all-or-nothing law and has no refractory period.

questions.stem: About the ionic mechanisms of postsynaptic potentials:
options: The IPSP can result from an exit of K⁺ from the cell
The EPSP results from a simultaneous increase in gNa⁺ and gK⁺
The IPSP results from an entry of Na⁺ into the cell
The IPSP can result from an entry of Cl⁻ into the cell
questions.explanation: EPSP: simultaneous increase in gNa⁺ and gK⁺. IPSP: hyperpolarization by Cl⁻ entry and/or K⁺ exit. Na⁺ entry would depolarize.

questions.stem: Binding of GABA to its receptors on a postsynaptic neuron:
options: Depolarizes the postsynaptic membrane
Produces a hyperpolarization of the postsynaptic membrane
Produces a potential that is the mirror image of the EPSP
Opens channels through which Cl⁻ enters the cell
questions.explanation: GABA is inhibitory: the IPSP is a hyperpolarization, mirror image of the EPSP, here due to Cl⁻ entry through transmitter-gated channels.

questions.stem: About synaptic integration in the postsynaptic neuron:
options: An action potential is triggered when the sum of EPSPs exceeds threshold at the initial segment
Membrane excitability is maximal at the initial segment
This is due to the abundance of voltage-dependent Na⁺ channels there
The initial segment (trigger zone) is where the neuronal action potential is born
questions.explanation: All are stated in the course: the trigger zone is rich in voltage-dependent Na⁺ channels, so summed EPSPs that exceed threshold there give rise to an AP.

questions.stem: The figure shows potentials recorded at the end-plate of a muscle fiber after motor-nerve stimulation, in the normal state and after Na⁺ channel blockade.
options: Curve Y is a propagated muscle action potential
Curves X are end-plate potentials, local depolarizations
The dashed line corresponds to the resting potential of the muscle fiber
Curves X were recorded in the normal state, without any blockade
questions.explanation: Normally nerve stimulation always triggers a muscle AP (Y). With Na⁺ channels blocked only the local EPP remains (X). The dashed line is the trigger threshold (≈ −60 mV); rest is ≈ −75 mV.

questions.stem: In a neuro-neuronal synapse:
options: Glutamate binding to transmitter-gated channels lets Na⁺ in and produces an EPSP
Neurotransmitter release requires calcium entry into the presynaptic terminal
The EPSP is a depolarization of the presynaptic membrane
The neurotransmitter is always acetylcholine
questions.explanation: The EPSP is a postsynaptic depolarization (e.g. glutamate opening Na⁺-permeable channels). Release depends on presynaptic Ca²⁺ entry. Many mediators exist (glutamate, GABA, dopamine…), not only ACh.
